notes.text: To lead us to Providence, acknowledging God in all our ways;

To lead to Christ, who descended from Ruth, and part of whose genealogy concludes the book Naomi removes to Moab, ver. 1, 2. Her husband and sons die, ver. 3-5. Designing to return to Bethlehem, she addresses her daughters-in-law, ver. 6-13. Orpah stays, but Ruth returns with her, ver. 14-18. They came to Bethlehem, ver. 19-22.
Took wives — Either these were Proselytes when they married them, or they sinned in marrying them, and therefore were punished with short life, and want of issue.

Was left of her two sons, and her husband — Loss of children and widowhood are both come upon her. By whom shall she be comforted? It is God alone that is able to comfort those who are thus cast down.
Bread — That is, food; so she staid no longer there than necessity forced her.

Mother's house — Because daughters used to converse more frequently with their mothers, and to dwell in the same apartments with them, which then were distinct from those parts of the house where the men dwelt. The dead - With my sons, your husbands, while they lived.

Your husbands — According to the ancient custom, Gen. xxxviii, 8, and the express law of God, Deut. xxv, 5, which doubtless she had acquainted them with before, among other branches of the Jewish religion.

It grieveth me — That you are left without the comfort of husbands or children; that I must part with such affectionate daughters; and that my circumstances are such, that I cannot invite you to go alone with me. For her condition was so mean at this time, that Ruth, when she came to her mother's city, was forced to glean for a living. It is with me, that God has a controversy. This language becomes us, when we are under affliction; tho' many others share in the trouble, yet we are to hear the voice of the rod, as if it spake only to us. But did not she wish to bring them to the worship of the God of Israel? Undoubtedly she did. But she would have them first consider upon what terms, lest having set their hand to the plow, they should look back.

Kissed — Departed from her with a kiss. Bade her farewell forever. She loved Naomi, but she did not love her so well, as to quit her country for her sake. Thus many have a value for Christ, and yet come short of salvation by him, because they cannot find in their hearts, to forsake other things for him. They love him, and yet leave him, because they do not love him enough, but love other things better.

To her gods — Those that forsake the communion of saints, will certainly break off their communion with God. This she saith, to try Ruth's sincerity and constancy, and that she might intimate to her, that if she went with her, she must embrace the true religion.

There will I be buried — Not desiring to have so much as her dead body carried back into the land of Moab: but Naomi and she having joined souls, she desires they may mingle dust, in hopes of rising together, and remaining together forver. 18. Left speaking unto her - See the power of resolution! Those who are half- resolved, are like a door a-jar, which invites a thief. But resolution shuts and bolts he door, and then the devil flees from us.

glossa.text:
*It came to pass.* Because of the scarcity of spiritual teachers to whom the authority of judging is given, there came a famine of the word of God, when the law also had been corrupted through Jewish traditions.

*And the man went away,* ((RAB.)) Christ, that is, born in Bethlehem of Juda, visited the pilgrimage of this world with his wife, that is, the Church, and with two children, that is, with the two orders of prophets and apostles, who by the blood of Christ were freed from the servitude of sin.

*The man went away.* ((RAB.)) Whom certain men understand to be the Decalogue of the law, and his wife the synagogue, and his two sons the royal honour and the priestly: which acquired to themselves a bond not only among the people of the Jews, but of the proselytes also, as was done in the time of David and of Solomon and of others.

*Mahalon.* He who is from the window, or from the beginning. This is the choir of the prophets, through whom the light of faith first went forth into the world from the window: who were also the first preachers of the true light, that is, of Christ.

*Chelion,* consummation. These are the apostles, who brought the riddles of the prophets to the consummation of full understanding. These are rightly Ephrathites, sprung from Bethlehem of Juda: who, filled with the bread of heaven, gathered the fruit of their preaching through the preaching of the Gospel. For Ephrathite is interpreted fruitful, Bethlehem the house of bread, Juda confession; whence: *Give ye them the hand.* Likewise, *Going, preach ye the Gospel of the kingdom of God.* And elsewhere: *I have chosen you out of the world, that you should go and bring forth fruit ((Marc. VI, XVI; Joan. XVI))*.

*Ruth.* She is interpreted seeing, or hastening, or failing: in whom the obedience and the belief of the Gentiles is designated, of whom it is said: *A people which I knew not hath served me,* etc. And elsewhere: *Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God ((Psal. LXVI))*. Two peoples therefore were called through the holy preachers to the fellowship of the faith and of the elect of God, that out of diverse flocks there might be made one fold.

*They died.* After the completion of their holy labour, that is, they passed over from the exile of this world to the heavenly kingdoms, so that, the commandment of the Decalogue being fulfilled, they might receive the penny of blessedness.

*She went out,* etc., *both of them.* The Church busily takes pains to lead the peoples, whom the Apostles and the prophets instructed in their own time, to the unity of faith and to the fellowship of the Christian religion: she who has learned, on the report of Scripture, that the just man shall not be forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread — the bread which came down from heaven ((Psal. XXXVI)).

*Go into the house.* The Church does not act without discernment, nor receive anyone without discernment, whence: *Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits, whether they be of God ((I Joan. IV))*. These things can also fit the synagogue, which draws back those who are coming to the faith of Christ, and most of all this: that, overcome by the truth, she acknowledges herself too weak for child-bearing: *Return, my daughters.*

*Shall I have any more.* ((RAB.)) The voice of the synagogue confessing the truth and not keeping silence about the guilt that has come upon her: who, forsaken by her husband, that is, by David, and deprived of her sons, that is, of kings and princes, confesses after the coming of Christ that she is barren and too weak to conceive sons for God.

*She lifted up.* By these women — of whom the one, grieving and mourning, goes back from her mother-in-law, while the other clings to her with obstinate mind — believers are signified: of whom some, when the grace of baptism and its fellowship has been received, slip back into their former errors, whom Orpha signifies, who returned to her own gods; but others, with settled purpose, take possession of the grace they have received, whom Ruth signifies.

*Whithersoever.* So the Church, called out of the Gentiles, her country left behind — that is, idolatry given up, and the fleshly manner of life and its desires — professes that God is her own, in whom the saints have believed, and that she will go where the flesh of Christ ascended, and for his name will suffer in this world even unto death, and be with the people of the saints and of the prophets and of the patriarchs; whence: *Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people ((Rom. XV))*.

*Seeing.* The Gentile people follows the preachers with obstinate mind into the holy land, and into the city of God, Bethlehem, where it is made ready to receive the bridegroom born of the stock of Abraham, in whom all the nations, or tribes, of the earth shall be blessed.

notes.text: That day — As soon as ever he is dead. Thoughts - All his designs and endeavours either for himself or for others.

For ever — Both because he liveth forever to fulfil his promises, and because he is eternally faithful. The psalmist praises God for his care over the church, ver. 1-14. His government over all, ver. 15-18. His giving his word to Israel, ver. 19, 20.

glossa.text: *Alleluia.* ((CAS.)) This voice, as it were saving musics *musicas*; read *musica*, "a saving music", like a heavenly harmony, which delights not men only but angels also, setting forth the praise of God. And it is fitly prefixed to this psalm, where the just man exhorts his soul to the praise of God: because in adversities the soul is sometimes troubled, whether it will or no. Whence above: *Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?* But that he may take away her disquiet, he suggests joy out of hope, if not out of the thing itself: *Hope in God,* etc. ((AUG.)) This soul, lifted up by hope, praises God here. ((CAS.)) First, he counsels himself, as it were all men, to praise, lest prayer be made among vain things; and as though acquiescing in the counsel, he affirms that he will praise there where he shall be able to praise fully. Secondly, he admonishes others not to hope in man, there: *Trust not.* Thirdly, he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, there: *Blessed,* etc.

*Praise the Lord, O my soul.* But it is asked, by whom, and to whom, is this counsel given? If it be said that the flesh counsels the soul, this does not seem to be true, since counsel is wont to be given by the better and the worthier to the inferior: but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For the soul, although it be blamed because it is a sinner, is nevertheless called better by nature than the body that is praised in its own kind, because a spiritual nature excels the body, which it moves, rules, endows with sense, and apprehends: and being itself unbounded, it is near to the substance of God. So gold, blamed because it is foul, surpasses lead in purity, praise *laudatio*; read *laudato*, "that is praised": so too a bad man surpasses the best of horses. Counsel therefore is not given to the soul by the flesh, however greatly it be subdued and made peaceable: which nevertheless is dead because of sin. Nor yet does the mortal flesh counsel the immortal soul, because it is always beneath the soul; but the higher part of the soul, that is, the mind, which thinks upon the divine wisdom, cleaving to it and sighing after it, sees certain of its own parts troubled by the motions of the world, and hurried away to outward things by the desire of earthly goods: whence it calls it back to things inward and higher. Exhorting itself therefore according to its sensuality, it says: *Praise the Lord, O my soul.* For what pleases thee in this world? Divided among so many loves of the things of the ages, gather thyself to thy Author: here is peace and security for thee. Then the soul answers the mind, as one weighed down here and not able to leave off, as is meet. *I will praise in life.* Here in death I shall praise but thinly, because the body *is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the sense that thinketh upon many things ((Sap. IX))*; here hope feeds us, life is in the world to come.

*In my life.* ((CAS.)) When I shall have cleaved to him perfectly, from whom to be parted, as now befalls, is death: but hope consoles, in which, living after a sort, it praises.

*As long as.* Not that at some time he shall not be, because he shall be for ever, and therefore truly long.

*Trust not,* etc. ((CAS.)) The second part. The counsel being given and confirmed, where he shall be able to praise fully, he admonishes them, as though set far off, and in the meantime while evils last (by which the soul is troubled), not to hope in man, but in God. ((AUG.)) Or, as one set in mind at the end of the world: he teaches them not to love things soon to end in place of things eternal; as if by my example also, *trust not,* etc. *In the children of men.* ((ID.)) In one son of man is salvation, and in him do ye hope. Not because he is a son of man, but because he is the Son of God. Not for that which he took from thee, but for that which he kept in himself.
*His spirit shall go forth,* etc. ((CAS.)) First he cleanses hearts by forbidding what is hurtful, that afterward he may aim at what is saving by admonishing to wholesome things.

*Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob.* ((CAS.)) The third part, where he teaches that the whole hope is to be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes from his works, that the Gentile world, so often confuted, may be still. ((AUG.)) Hurtful things being removed, he teaches what belongs to salvation, namely, in whom hope is to be placed. *His helper is his hope.* ((CAS.)) Of that Jacob himself he was so the helper, etc., *as far as* that is, of this true Jacob, as of that one.

*Who made heaven and earth.* ((ID.)) Because the worshippers of demons also have hope in their god, he determines in whom hope ought to be, that is, in Christ, and this he shows even to the end of the psalm, describing him through all things. *All things that are in them.* Lest thou think any other to be the creator, or that there exists a creator even of the smallest things.

*Who keepeth truth for ever.* ((CAS.)) Christ, who is the truth; every man is a liar. *He executeth judgment.* These two pertain to justice. Christ the judge avenges those who suffer for his name, and gives food to them that love him. *For them that suffer wrong.* ((AUG.)) Not every trouble is a wrong. What thou sufferest by right is not a wrong, as is that which the robber and other wicked men suffer. It is one thing therefore to suffer wrong, another to suffer punishment. For a man suffers punishment by right, but wrong is contrary to right.

*The Lord looseth them that are fettered.* ((CAS.)) This belongs to the abundance of his sweetness.

*The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down.* Whom the devil casts down, the Lord lifts up.

*He loveth the just.* ((CAS.)) Whom he sets in eternal blessedness.

*The fatherless and the widow he will receive.* *suseipiet* ((AUG.)) The whole Church of the Gentiles is come as a stranger to the fathers, a daughter not by flesh but by imitation.

*The fatherless* are all who are in pilgrimage, whose father is absent; and every faithful soul is a *widow* while the bridegroom is absent: whence they desire the more both the father and the bridegroom, and God protects them, not seen but desired.

*The Lord shall reign for ever.* ((CAS.)) This is of his magnificence.

He shall reign in us when our hearts shall be firm in him, which is not yet.

notes.text: An high priest of good things to come — Described, ver. 15. Entered through a greater, that is, a more noble, and perfect tabernacle - Namely, his own body. Not of this creation - Not framed by man, as that tabernacle was.
The holy place — Heaven. For us - All that believe.

If the ashes of an heifer — Consumed by fire as a sin-offering, being sprinkled on them who were legally unclean. Purified the flesh - Removed that legal uncleanness, and re-admitted them to the temple and the congregation. Num. xix, 17, 18, 19.

How much more shall the blood of Christ. — The merit of all his sufferings. Who through the eternal Spirit - The work of redemption being the work of the whole Trinity. Neither is the Second Person alone concerned even in the amazing condescension that was needful to complete it. The Father delivers up the kingdom to the Son; and the Holy Ghost becomes the gift of the Messiah, being, as it were, sent according to his good pleasure. Offered himself - Infinitely more precious than any created victim, and that without spot to God. Purge our conscience - Our inmost soul. From dead works - From all the inward and outward works of the devil, which spring from spiritual death in the soul, and lead to death everlasting. To serve the living God - In the life of faith, in perfect love and spotless holiness.

glossa.text: *By a greater.* Christ entered the tabernacle, that is, heaven. By the name of the sign, that is, of the tabernacle, the Apostle designates the thing signified, that is, heaven, which is well called, *by a greater,* because it holds more than that earthly one, and *more perfect,* because there is perfect blessedness.
*Into the holies.* He expounds what he had said: *A tabernacle not made with hands, the holy of holies,* that is, heavenly things.

*For if the blood.* That through Christ there could be redemption, he proves from the lesser, because through those things of the law there was made a bodily cleansing. *Of goats.* The goat signifies Christ, through the likeness of the flesh of sin. Christ is called a bull, because with the horns of the two Testaments he tosses his enemies. *Unto the cleansing of the flesh,* that is, that the flesh might be cleansed on account of the precept of the law; but in Christ is perfection.

*He offered himself.* Christ, the mediator between God and men, is the giver of the New Testament: as high priest he is to us the giver of the new law. *Unspotted.* His blood is unspotted.

*From dead works;* that is, sins, which he who touches is defiled, as he who touched a dead body was defiled; nor does he enter into heaven, as neither did that man into the temple. *To the living.* Yet the death of Christ was necessary in the redemption not only of the Gentiles, but also of those transgressions which the law showed, it did not loose. So great was our sin, that we could not be saved unless the Only-begotten of God should die for us, who were debtors of death; but so he made us worthy of the Testament and of the promised inheritance, and thus the Testament was made firm.

notes.text: Which is the first commandment? — The principal, and most necessary to be observed. Matt. xxii, 34; Luke x, 25.

The Lord our God is one Lord — This is the foundation of the first commandment, yea, of all the commandments. The Lord our God, the Lord, the God of all men, is one God, essentially, though three persons. From this unity of God it follows, that we owe all our love to him alone. Deut. vi, 4.
With all thy strength — That is, the whole strength and capacity of thy understanding, will, and affections.
The second is like unto it — Of a like comprehensive nature: comprising our whole duty to man. There is no other moral, much less ceremonial commandment, greater than these. Lev. xix, 18.

To love him with all the heart — To love and serve him, with all the united powers of the soul in their utmost vigour; and to love his neighbour as himself - To maintain the same equitable and charitable temper and behaviour toward all men, as we, in like circumstances, would wish for from them toward ourselves, is a more necessary and important duty, than the offering the most noble and costly sacrifices.
Jesus said to him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God — Reader, art not thou? then go on: be a real Christian: else it had been better for thee to have been afar off.

glossa.text:
*He asked him. ((HIER.))* What does this question mean, since all who are skilled in the law know it? But the commandments are ordered differently in Exodus and in Leviticus and in Deuteronomy. For our infancy is nourished from these two breasts raised upon the bosom of the bride.

*The first of all,* etc. The greatest thing, which before all we ought to set in the heart as the one foundation of piety, is this, namely, the knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the carrying out of the divine working, which is perfected in the love of God and of the neighbour: this is *the faith which worketh by love.*

*Well, master. ((BEDA.))* The scribe shows in this answer that a weighty question had long been debated among the scribes and the Pharisees, etc., *as far as* but no one without faith and love, in which judgment this scribe declares himself to have been.

*Thou art not far from the kingdom of God,* etc. ((ISID.)) Although he had come to tempt: for ignorance is farther off than knowledge, as it is said to the Sadducees: *You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God ((Matth. XXII))*. ((BEDA.)) Matthew says that he asked by way of tempting, etc., *as far as* according to that word: *He that believeth easily is light of heart, and shall be made less ((Eccl. XIX))*.

*And no man.* Because they are confuted in words, they question him no more; but, having openly seized him, they deliver him to the Roman power, whence it appears that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but hardly be quiet.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.id: Modern Beit Lahm c. 8 km south of Jerusalem in the central hill country. Distinct from the Galilean Bethlehem of Joshua 19:15 (Beit Lahm of Zebulun). Burial place of Rachel (Gen 35:19, given as Ephrath); home of the Boaz-Obed-Jesse-David line; in later tradition the birthplace of Jesus.

places.name: Moab
places.id: The plateau east of the Dead Sea, traditionally bounded by the Arnon canyon (south, against Edom) and the Heshbon plateau (north, against the trans-Jordan tribes). Ancestrally descended from Lot (Gen 19:37). Home of the Moabite Stone (Mesha Stele) found at Dhiban in 1868. Pin sits in the central plateau.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.’
echoes.note: Moses' words at Sinai, inaugurating the first covenant in blood. Hebrews quotes them to make blood the necessary seal of any covenant — and so to read Christ's death as the blood that ratifies the new one: ‘apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.’

echoes.text: Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar. He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that Yahweh has spoken will we do, and be obedient.” Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: Beyond the quoted clause (v. 8), the whole narrative frame of vv. 19–20 — Moses reading ‘every commandment to all the people,’ then sprinkling — retells Exod 24:6–8. Hebrews adds details (water, scarlet wool, hyssop, sprinkling the book) not in Exod 24, conflating it with the purification rites (Num 19; Lev 14): high recurrence of the sprinkling motif drives the link.

echoes.text: “A man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay them up outside of the camp in a clean place; and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for use in water for cleansing impurity. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: ‘The ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled’ (v. 13) names the red-heifer rite of Num 19:9. Strong verbal volume (‘ashes of the heifer… cleansing impurity’) and exact thematic coherence: an outward cleansing ‘of the flesh’ that Hebrews contrasts with the inward cleansing of conscience by Christ's blood.

echoes.text: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there...
echoes.note: The mechanics of v. 13 (ashes + water sprinkled on the defiled) and the ‘water… and hyssop’ of vv. 19–21 echo Num 19:17–18, where hyssop dips the ash-water and sprinkles ‘the tent, all the vessels, the persons.’ Hebrews' phrase ‘sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels’ tracks this list closely — recurrence of sprinkling vocabulary.

echoes.text: The priest shall take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet, and cast it into the middle of the burning of the heifer.
echoes.note: ‘With water and scarlet wool and hyssop’ (v. 19) imports the ‘hyssop and scarlet’ of the heifer rite (Num 19:6) into the retelling of the Sinai covenant-cutting, which had neither. The conflation shows Hebrews reading all the blood-rites as one figural system; verbal contact on ‘scarlet… hyssop’ is the tell.
echoes.altSource: Leviticus 14:4–6 (scarlet and hyssop in the cleansing of the leper)

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: ‘Apart from shedding of blood there is no remission’ (v. 22) crystallizes the principle of Lev 17:11 — blood makes atonement because the life is in it. No verbatim quotation, but high thematic coherence: this is the axiom on which the whole sacrificial argument of vv. 11–22 rests.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘The blood of goats and calves’ / ‘goats and bulls’ (vv. 12–13, 19) generalizes the Day-of-Atonement victims (bull and goat, Lev 16:3, 5–15). Faint and diffuse — Hebrews blends Day-of-Atonement animals with covenant-inauguration animals (Exod 24) — so verbal volume is low and the source is one strand among several.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: Jesus names the greatest commandment by quoting the Shema in full: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.' This is a formal, explicit citation of Israel's central confession, the pericope's anchor text.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The second commandment, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' is quoted verbatim from the Holiness Code. Mark's pairing of Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 as the summary of the Law is a formal double citation that the scribe affirms.

echoes.text: It was shown to you so that you might know that Yahweh is God. There is no one else besides him.
echoes.note: The scribe's approving gloss, 'he is one, and there is no other but he,' echoes Deuteronomy's monotheistic confession 'the Lord is God; there is no other besides him.' This buttresses the Shema's 'the Lord is one' with the classic Deuteronomic affirmation of God's uniqueness.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: The scribe declares that loving God and neighbor is 'more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices,' echoing Samuel's rebuke that 'to obey is better than sacrifice.' The prioritizing of covenant love and obedience over cultic offering is a prophetic commonplace the scribe deliberately invokes.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Hosea's 'I desire mercy/steadfast love, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings' lies directly behind the scribe's ranking of love above 'whole burnt offerings.' The pairing of love-of-God with the relativizing of burnt offerings closely matches Hosea's formula.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.
echoes.note: Deutero-Isaiah's repeated 'there is no other God besides me' supplies the same monotheistic formula the scribe uses ('there is none other but he'). Given the recurrence of this oneness language across Deuteronomy and Isaiah, the scribe's confession may draw on the broader prophetic monotheism as well as the Shema.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's contrast between multiplied burnt offerings and the real requirement to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God supplies the same prophetic logic the scribe applies. It belongs to the recurrent prophetic critique that ethical love outweighs sacrifice, reinforcing the scribe's verdict.

echoes.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
echoes.note: Joshua's exhortation to love the Lord, walk in his ways, and serve him 'with all your heart and all your soul' echoes the Shema's totalizing love-language that Jesus quotes. As a near-verbatim restatement of Deuteronomy's command, it shows the formula's currency but adds little beyond the primary citation.

notes.text: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart — And is this only an external commandment? Can any then say, that the Sinai - covenant was merely external? With all thy heart - With an entire love. He is One; therefore our hearts must be united in his love. And the whole stream of our affections must run toward Him. O that this love of God may be shed abroad in our hearts.

Teach them diligently — Hebrew. whet, or sharpen them, so as they may pierce deep into their hearts. This metaphor signifies the manner of instructing them, that it is to be done diligently, earnestly, frequently, discreetly.

Thou shalt bind them — Thou shalt give all diligence, and use all means to keep them in thy remembrance, as men often bind something upon their hands, or put it before their eyes to prevent forgetfulness of a thing which they much desire to remember.

glossa.text:
*Thou shalt love the Lord. ((AUG., lib. I de Doctrina Christiana, c. 26, 27, 28.))* Charity shall not be taken away, etc., *as far as* who by the opportunity of places and of times, or of any things whatsoever, are more closely joined to us.

*((GREG., lib. VII Moral., cap. 10.)) Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,* etc. Through the love of God is begotten the love of the neighbour, etc., *as far as* for in good things a friend is not known, and in evil things an enemy is not hidden.

The soul is of a threefold nature: therefore it is bidden to love in a threefold manner. God wills not that his love be divided, so that we should love at once God, and gold, or wife, or children. *No man can serve two masters ((Matth. VI))*; he himself is to be loved above all things, his love is set first.

*And thou shalt bind them as a sign.* The Pharisees, misinterpreting this, wrote the decalogue (that is, the ten words) upon little parchments, and carried them bound upon the forehead. Which the Babylonians do to this day, that they may be thought religious. Whence: *For they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge their fringes ((Matth. XXIII))*.

notes.text: Respect — A due respect, which implies hearty affection, diligent study, and constant practice. To all - So as not to allow myself in any known sin, or in the neglect of any known duty.
When — When by thy good spirit I shall he more fitly instructed in the meaning of thy word.
Forsake me not — For then I shall fall into the foulest sins.

An high priest of good things to come — Described, ver. 15. Entered through a greater, that is, a more noble, and perfect tabernacle - Namely, his own body. Not of this creation - Not framed by man, as that tabernacle was.
The holy place — Heaven. For us - All that believe.

If the ashes of an heifer — Consumed by fire as a sin-offering, being sprinkled on them who were legally unclean. Purified the flesh - Removed that legal uncleanness, and re-admitted them to the temple and the congregation. Num. xix, 17, 18, 19.

How much more shall the blood of Christ. — The merit of all his sufferings. Who through the eternal Spirit - The work of redemption being the work of the whole Trinity. Neither is the Second Person alone concerned even in the amazing condescension that was needful to complete it. The Father delivers up the kingdom to the Son; and the Holy Ghost becomes the gift of the Messiah, being, as it were, sent according to his good pleasure. Offered himself - Infinitely more precious than any created victim, and that without spot to God. Purge our conscience - Our inmost soul. From dead works - From all the inward and outward works of the devil, which spring from spiritual death in the soul, and lead to death everlasting. To serve the living God - In the life of faith, in perfect love and spotless holiness.

glossa.text: *By a greater.* Christ entered the tabernacle, that is, heaven. By the name of the sign, that is, of the tabernacle, the Apostle designates the thing signified, that is, heaven, which is well called, *by a greater,* because it holds more than that earthly one, and *more perfect,* because there is perfect blessedness.
*Into the holies.* He expounds what he had said: *A tabernacle not made with hands, the holy of holies,* that is, heavenly things.

*For if the blood.* That through Christ there could be redemption, he proves from the lesser, because through those things of the law there was made a bodily cleansing. *Of goats.* The goat signifies Christ, through the likeness of the flesh of sin. Christ is called a bull, because with the horns of the two Testaments he tosses his enemies. *Unto the cleansing of the flesh,* that is, that the flesh might be cleansed on account of the precept of the law; but in Christ is perfection.

*He offered himself.* Christ, the mediator between God and men, is the giver of the New Testament: as high priest he is to us the giver of the new law. *Unspotted.* His blood is unspotted.

*From dead works;* that is, sins, which he who touches is defiled, as he who touched a dead body was defiled; nor does he enter into heaven, as neither did that man into the temple. *To the living.* Yet the death of Christ was necessary in the redemption not only of the Gentiles, but also of those transgressions which the law showed, it did not loose. So great was our sin, that we could not be saved unless the Only-begotten of God should die for us, who were debtors of death; but so he made us worthy of the Testament and of the promised inheritance, and thus the Testament was made firm.

notes.text: Which is the first commandment? — The principal, and most necessary to be observed. Matt. xxii, 34; Luke x, 25.

The Lord our God is one Lord — This is the foundation of the first commandment, yea, of all the commandments. The Lord our God, the Lord, the God of all men, is one God, essentially, though three persons. From this unity of God it follows, that we owe all our love to him alone. Deut. vi, 4.
With all thy strength — That is, the whole strength and capacity of thy understanding, will, and affections.
The second is like unto it — Of a like comprehensive nature: comprising our whole duty to man. There is no other moral, much less ceremonial commandment, greater than these. Lev. xix, 18.

To love him with all the heart — To love and serve him, with all the united powers of the soul in their utmost vigour; and to love his neighbour as himself - To maintain the same equitable and charitable temper and behaviour toward all men, as we, in like circumstances, would wish for from them toward ourselves, is a more necessary and important duty, than the offering the most noble and costly sacrifices.
Jesus said to him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God — Reader, art not thou? then go on: be a real Christian: else it had been better for thee to have been afar off.

glossa.text:
*He asked him. ((HIER.))* What does this question mean, since all who are skilled in the law know it? But the commandments are ordered differently in Exodus and in Leviticus and in Deuteronomy. For our infancy is nourished from these two breasts raised upon the bosom of the bride.

*The first of all,* etc. The greatest thing, which before all we ought to set in the heart as the one foundation of piety, is this, namely, the knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the carrying out of the divine working, which is perfected in the love of God and of the neighbour: this is *the faith which worketh by love.*

*Well, master. ((BEDA.))* The scribe shows in this answer that a weighty question had long been debated among the scribes and the Pharisees, etc., *as far as* but no one without faith and love, in which judgment this scribe declares himself to have been.

*Thou art not far from the kingdom of God,* etc. ((ISID.)) Although he had come to tempt: for ignorance is farther off than knowledge, as it is said to the Sadducees: *You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God ((Matth. XXII))*. ((BEDA.)) Matthew says that he asked by way of tempting, etc., *as far as* according to that word: *He that believeth easily is light of heart, and shall be made less ((Eccl. XIX))*.

*And no man.* Because they are confuted in words, they question him no more; but, having openly seized him, they deliver him to the Roman power, whence it appears that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but hardly be quiet.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.’
echoes.note: Moses' words at Sinai, inaugurating the first covenant in blood. Hebrews quotes them to make blood the necessary seal of any covenant — and so to read Christ's death as the blood that ratifies the new one: ‘apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.’

echoes.text: Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar. He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that Yahweh has spoken will we do, and be obedient.” Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: Beyond the quoted clause (v. 8), the whole narrative frame of vv. 19–20 — Moses reading ‘every commandment to all the people,’ then sprinkling — retells Exod 24:6–8. Hebrews adds details (water, scarlet wool, hyssop, sprinkling the book) not in Exod 24, conflating it with the purification rites (Num 19; Lev 14): high recurrence of the sprinkling motif drives the link.

echoes.text: “A man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay them up outside of the camp in a clean place; and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for use in water for cleansing impurity. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: ‘The ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled’ (v. 13) names the red-heifer rite of Num 19:9. Strong verbal volume (‘ashes of the heifer… cleansing impurity’) and exact thematic coherence: an outward cleansing ‘of the flesh’ that Hebrews contrasts with the inward cleansing of conscience by Christ's blood.

echoes.text: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there...
echoes.note: The mechanics of v. 13 (ashes + water sprinkled on the defiled) and the ‘water… and hyssop’ of vv. 19–21 echo Num 19:17–18, where hyssop dips the ash-water and sprinkles ‘the tent, all the vessels, the persons.’ Hebrews' phrase ‘sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels’ tracks this list closely — recurrence of sprinkling vocabulary.

echoes.text: The priest shall take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet, and cast it into the middle of the burning of the heifer.
echoes.note: ‘With water and scarlet wool and hyssop’ (v. 19) imports the ‘hyssop and scarlet’ of the heifer rite (Num 19:6) into the retelling of the Sinai covenant-cutting, which had neither. The conflation shows Hebrews reading all the blood-rites as one figural system; verbal contact on ‘scarlet… hyssop’ is the tell.
echoes.altSource: Leviticus 14:4–6 (scarlet and hyssop in the cleansing of the leper)

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: ‘Apart from shedding of blood there is no remission’ (v. 22) crystallizes the principle of Lev 17:11 — blood makes atonement because the life is in it. No verbatim quotation, but high thematic coherence: this is the axiom on which the whole sacrificial argument of vv. 11–22 rests.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘The blood of goats and calves’ / ‘goats and bulls’ (vv. 12–13, 19) generalizes the Day-of-Atonement victims (bull and goat, Lev 16:3, 5–15). Faint and diffuse — Hebrews blends Day-of-Atonement animals with covenant-inauguration animals (Exod 24) — so verbal volume is low and the source is one strand among several.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: Jesus names the greatest commandment by quoting the Shema in full: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.' This is a formal, explicit citation of Israel's central confession, the pericope's anchor text.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The second commandment, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' is quoted verbatim from the Holiness Code. Mark's pairing of Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 as the summary of the Law is a formal double citation that the scribe affirms.

echoes.text: It was shown to you so that you might know that Yahweh is God. There is no one else besides him.
echoes.note: The scribe's approving gloss, 'he is one, and there is no other but he,' echoes Deuteronomy's monotheistic confession 'the Lord is God; there is no other besides him.' This buttresses the Shema's 'the Lord is one' with the classic Deuteronomic affirmation of God's uniqueness.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: The scribe declares that loving God and neighbor is 'more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices,' echoing Samuel's rebuke that 'to obey is better than sacrifice.' The prioritizing of covenant love and obedience over cultic offering is a prophetic commonplace the scribe deliberately invokes.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Hosea's 'I desire mercy/steadfast love, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings' lies directly behind the scribe's ranking of love above 'whole burnt offerings.' The pairing of love-of-God with the relativizing of burnt offerings closely matches Hosea's formula.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.
echoes.note: Deutero-Isaiah's repeated 'there is no other God besides me' supplies the same monotheistic formula the scribe uses ('there is none other but he'). Given the recurrence of this oneness language across Deuteronomy and Isaiah, the scribe's confession may draw on the broader prophetic monotheism as well as the Shema.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's contrast between multiplied burnt offerings and the real requirement to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God supplies the same prophetic logic the scribe applies. It belongs to the recurrent prophetic critique that ethical love outweighs sacrifice, reinforcing the scribe's verdict.

echoes.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
echoes.note: Joshua's exhortation to love the Lord, walk in his ways, and serve him 'with all your heart and all your soul' echoes the Shema's totalizing love-language that Jesus quotes. As a near-verbatim restatement of Deuteronomy's command, it shows the formula's currency but adds little beyond the primary citation.

lines: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
We will love the Lord with all our heart.
And the second is like it:
love your neighbor as yourself.
On these two hang the whole of the law.
We are not far from the kingdom of God.
Come, let us worship with heart and soul and strength.
We come to love God and neighbor. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A scribe asked, Which commandment is the first of all? And Jesus answered with the words Israel has carried since Moses: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart.
Bind these words on your hand, write them on your doorposts, teach them to your children, keep them close as breath.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart.
And do not stop there, he said; the second is like it — you shall love your neighbor as yourself.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart.
You are not far from the kingdom. Come near now; bring your whole heart and soul and strength and worship.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. Amen.
